cross_tool_domains.attrition: Not applicable / Can't tell: Single-wave cross-sectional qualitative fieldwork conducted between June and August 2012 with no longitudinal follow-up; interview refusal or non-response rates are not reported.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High concern (uncontrolled qualitative case study): No counterfactual or analytical separation between the nascent Bonsucro certification process (pre-audits in eight mills in 2010, internal auditor training in 2011, zero pre-audits among Procana small suppliers, and pending appeals over water limits) and pre-existing drivers of land/water concentration, including 140 years of plantation monoculture, Colombian biofuel blend mandates, CVC regulatory capture, armed conflict, and El Nino droughts.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Adequate documentary specification, weak field compliance verification: Accurately identifies and critiques specific provisions of Bonsucro Version 3.0 (Principle 1 on national tenure law and ILO Convention 169 Articles 13-19; Principle 5 water-use thresholds of 20 kg water/kg sugar, 30 kg/kg ethanol, <130 kg/kg cane, and N/P fertilizer input metrics), EU RED (2009), Colombian Decree #4892 (2012), Law 99 (1993), and local potable-water rules (Decree 1541/78 and Agreement 042/2010), but relies on stakeholder perceptions rather than primary audit or administrative enforcement records and explicitly notes that verifying legal land use was beyond the study's scope.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Moderate-to-high concern / Can't tell: Primary data come from unstandardized exploratory interviews without reported interview guides, recording/transcription procedures, or translation protocols, paired with secondary regional statistics; household water-access impacts rely on unverified stakeholder accounts.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Weak primary measurement (secondary statistics plus qualitative accounts): No original hydrological or household survey measurements were collected; basin-level water allocation and pollution metrics (64% surface water and 88% groundwater concessions held by sugar producers; 76% of N/P/pesticide load) are cited secondarily from Perez et al. (2011) and CVC reports, while community dry-season water shortages and forced household water purchases are documented only via qualitative interview summaries.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Moderate concern: Although the paper juxtaposes industry association perspectives (Asocana, Procana) with critical agricultural researcher, small farmer, and rural resident accounts, the absence of a qualitative coding protocol or participant-by-category breakdown prevents verification against selective quotation.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Moderate-to-high concern / Can't tell: Relies on purposive selection of 14 exploratory interviewees across seven broad stakeholder groups in Valle del Cauca (plus an unspecified number of displaced rural community residents mentioned on p. 465) without reporting the sampling frame, recruitment mechanics, sample distribution across groups, or refusal rates.

domain_ratings.justification: The authors clearly state their research aim: using Ribot and Peluso's theory of access to examine how Colombia's historical, political-economic, and institutional context shapes the implementation of Bonsucro biofuel sustainability certification and whether certification legitimates or mitigates land and water grabs in Valle del Cauca.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the research design appropriate to address the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: The single-country/regional case study design focusing on Valle del Cauca in Colombia is explicitly justified by Colombia's status as a major Latin American biofuel producer with state blend mandates, entrenched agrarian inequality, armed conflict, and active early engagement by Asocana and Procana with Bonsucro standards. However, because Bonsucro certification was still in pre-audit/training stages during 2012 fieldwork, claims about certification outcomes remain partly prospective.

domain_ratings.justification: While the authors state that 14 stakeholders were purposively selected to capture diverse perspectives (farmers, union activists, local government officials, sugar industry associations, sugar refineries, and research agronomists), they do not explain how participants were identified or contacted, how many interviewees belonged to each group, whether anyone declined, or whether the 'other residents in rural communities' mentioned on PDF p. 11 (p. 465) were included within or additional to the 14 interviewees.

domain_ratings.justification: Quotations are attributed anonymously by general role (e.g., industry participant, small farmer, Asocana representative, agricultural researcher), which protects confidentiality in a setting involving allegations of corruption, money laundering, and paramilitary violence, and participants are thanked in the Acknowledgments. However, institutional ethics/IRB approval, informed consent procedures, and participant safety protections are not reported.

domain_ratings.justification: No analytical procedures (such as qualitative coding, thematic analysis, memo writing, inter-coder checks, or rules for selecting quotes and triangulating interview claims against secondary sources) are described. Although opposing perspectives from industry associations and critics/residents are presented, the rigor of transcript analysis cannot be verified, and the authors note in Footnote 6 that independent verification of legal land claims was outside the paper's scope.

domain_ratings.justification: Valuable conceptual and empirical contribution to agrifood/biofuel governance scholarship: it demonstrates how 'apolitical' metric-based transnational certification (Bonsucro Principles 1 and 5) can obscure historical land concentration, unequal CVC water concessions, downstream water pollution, and industry lobbying to reclassify potable groundwater as non-potable under Decree 1541/78 and Agreement 042/2010. Transferability and causal certainty are tempered by the small exploratory sample and incomplete implementation of Bonsucro certification at the time of fieldwork.
domain_ratings.rating: Valuable qualitative case study with clear conceptual insights into private certification limits, tempered by exploratory sampling and thin methodological reporting

overall_narrative_summary: Selfa, Bain, and Moreno (2014) present a primary qualitative case study examining how Colombia's political economy of land and water governance shapes the implementation and limits of Bonsucro sustainability certification in the Valle del Cauca sugarcane-ethanol sector. Because all quantitative figures in the paper (e.g., land Gini/ownership shares, CVC surface and groundwater concession shares, river nutrient loads) are cited from secondary sources rather than original quantitative data collection or analysis, the CASP Qualitative Checklist is the appropriate appraisal instrument. Methodological strengths include clearly articulated theoretical aims grounded in Ribot and Peluso's theory of access (Q1-Q3), detailed documentary scrutiny of Bonsucro Version 3.0 Principles 1 and 5 alongside national and regional water regulations (Decree 1541/78, Agreement 042/2010, Law 99 of 1993), and balanced presentation of contrasting narratives from industry associations (Asocana, Procana), critics, and rural residents (Q9-Q10). However, methodological reporting is sparse across core empirical procedures: recruitment mechanics and group-level sample counts for the 14 exploratory interviews (and their relation to rural community residents cited on p. 465) are unspecified (Q4: Can't tell); interview protocols, recording/transcription, and translation procedures are omitted (Q5: Can't tell); researcher reflexivity is absent (Q6: No); formal ethics/consent procedures are unreported despite sensitive conflict/corruption topics (Q7: Can't tell); and qualitative coding/analytic methods are not described (Q8: Can't tell). Moreover, because Bonsucro certification in Colombia was still in pre-audit and standard-negotiation stages in 2012, conclusions about certification reinforcing water and land grabs are partly prospective and cannot isolate Bonsucro's effect from long-standing state policies and CVC governance.
overall_rating: Moderate-to-high methodological concern (4 Can't tell items and 1 No item out of Q1-Q9)
study_design_identified: Primary qualitative case study (in-depth exploratory stakeholder interviews paired with documentary analysis of certification standards, laws, and secondary regional reports)
where_found_summary: Methods description in a single paragraph at the end of 'Biofuels, land and water grabs: prospects for governance' (PDF p. 4, p. 458), supplemented by brief mention of rural resident interviews in 'Water grabs and Bonsucro certification' (PDF p. 11, p. 465), scope limitation in Footnote 6 (PDF p. 8, p. 462), regulatory/standard analysis across PDF pp. 7-11 (pp. 461-465), and Acknowledgments/author bios (PDF pp. 13-14, pp. 467-468).
why_tool_chosen: The study's primary empirical component consists of in-depth exploratory qualitative interviews with 14 sugarcane/ethanol stakeholders (plus rural residents) in Valle del Cauca between June and August 2012, paired with qualitative documentary critique of Bonsucro standards and Colombian policies. All quantitative statistics on land concentration and water concessions/pollution are cited from secondary literature (e.g., Perez et al. 2011; Marin et al. 2011; CVC 2011; DANE 2012) rather than a primary quantitative empirical component, making the CASP Qualitative Checklist the exact matching tool rather than MMAT, JBI, or ROBINS-I.
